$comment: Rule catalog — calibration. Standard 3. Carries five of the nineteen prohibitions: unmeasured calibration claims, lookahead in generation and in evaluation, and outcome bias in both directions. Three of the five are manual-review, because no structure in a record can settle them.

rules.title: Calibration is not claimed unless it was measured
rules.description: A calibration score appears only when measured is true, and a measured claim names the method, the dataset, and when it was performed.
rules.rationale: Calibration is an empirical property: it means that among the times a method said 70 percent, the outcome happened about 70 percent of the time. That is a measurement someone performed on resolved outcomes, or it is nothing. A score with no measurement is a claim to have checked.
rules.remediation: Either record the measurement — method, dataset, date, metric, value — or set measured to false and remove the score.
rules.$assuranceNote: A structural check establishes that a measurement was DESCRIBED. It cannot establish that it was performed, that the dataset was out of sample, or that the reported value is the one that came out. Those need human review recorded as an attestation.

rules.title: A historical prediction uses no information from after its cutoff
rules.description: Where a record is a historical reconstruction, it declares an information cutoff, and every data source it draws on is as-of at or before that cutoff.
rules.rationale: A backtest that sees the future does not measure a prediction method, it measures hindsight, and it will report excellent performance that cannot be reproduced going forward. This is the most common way a prediction system convinces its owners it works.
rules.remediation: Set provenance.historical.informationCutoff and exclude every source whose asOf falls after it.
rules.$assuranceNote: The evaluator compares the declared asOf timestamps against the declared cutoff. It cannot detect information that leaked into a model through a source the record does not list, which is the harder and more common form of the error.

rules.title: Historical prediction quality is judged only on what was available at the time
rules.description: An assessment of how good a past prediction was uses only the information that existed when it was generated.
rules.rationale: Judging a past prediction with facts that emerged afterwards makes every prediction look careless in retrospect and teaches the wrong lesson. The question is whether the prediction was justified by what was knowable, not whether it matched what turned out to be true.
rules.remediation: Record the evaluation's own information boundary and confirm the assessment respected it. Attest to that review in the policy.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated evaluates this. It concerns how a person reasoned about a past prediction, which leaves no trace in the record. It is reported not-evaluated until a human attests, and it never passes by default.

rules.title: A correct outcome is not treated as proof the process was good
rules.description: No claim about the quality of a prediction process rests on the fact that a prediction came true.
rules.rationale: A method that assigns 5 percent to the thing that happens is not thereby vindicated, and a lucky call is indistinguishable from a good one on a sample of one. Systems that reward correct outcomes rather than good process drift toward confident extremes, because those are the calls that look brilliant when they land.
rules.remediation: Assess process quality over many predictions using a proper scoring rule, and attest to that review.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated evaluates this. The record schema deliberately carries no outcome field, so the reasoning this rule prohibits happens entirely outside the artifact. Human review only.

rules.title: An incorrect outcome is not treated as proof the prediction was bad
rules.description: No claim that a probabilistic prediction was wrong rests on the fact that the predicted outcome did not occur.
rules.rationale: The mirror of the rule above, and the more corrosive of the two in practice. A well-calibrated 80 percent prediction is supposed to be wrong one time in five. Treating each of those as a failure produces pressure to hedge every number toward the middle, which destroys the information the predictions carried.
rules.remediation: Judge the prediction against what was knowable when it was made, over a sample large enough to say anything. Attest to that review.
rules.$assuranceNote: Nothing automated evaluates this, for the same reason as its mirror: no outcome is recorded, so the error lives entirely in how people talk about resolved predictions. Human review only.
